query: For high-entropy-alloy protective coatings in wear-resistant applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their wear performance and why? Define a controlled change that would distinguish the hypothesis from a baseline, the directional observations expected if it is correct, the range over which it should hold, the prior evidence that supports it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Wear resistance in high-entropy alloy (HEA) protective coatings is primarily governed by precipitation strengthening; specifically, the formation of finely dispersed, nanoscale hard phase precipitates within a softer matrix enhances load transfer and retards plastic deformation during wear.
generation.material_initial_state: A near-stoichiometric HEA coating that forms continuous antiphase domains (APDs) with limited nanoscale precipitates.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled deviation in the alloy composition (within the range of Al < 25 at.% and Mn > 15 at.%) to promote the formation of nanoscale precipitates (e.g., L21 phase) rather than uniform APDs.
generation.conditions: Wear tests (e.g., pin-on-disk) under controlled loads and temperatures (from room temperature up to ~700 °C) ensuring similar processing procedures and surface finish for all coatings.
generation.structural_mediator: The induced nanoscale precipitates that form in a BCC matrix, in contrast to the continuous APDs formed in stoichiometric compositions.
generation.mechanism: Under tribological stress, the hard precipitates bear and transfer load from the surrounding ductile matrix, thereby obstructing dislocation motion and delaying crack initiation and propagation. This improved load-sharing and barrier effect reduce plastic deformation and lower wear rates.
generation.predicted_outcome: HEA coatings engineered to contain a high density of nanoscale precipitates should display increased hardness and a reduced wear rate compared to baseline coatings that form only APDs.
generation.baseline: HEA coatings with stoichiometric compositions that form predominantly APDs, resulting in lower load-transfer efficiency and higher wear rates.
generation.boundary: This effect is anticipated to hold for HEA systems within the studied compositional limits (e.g., Al < 25 at.% and Mn > 15 at.%) and for wear conditions up to moderate elevated temperatures (~700 °C).
generation.uncertainty: The optimal precipitate size, volume fraction, and dispersion for maximum wear resistance, as well as the detailed wear mechanisms under varying stress and temperature conditions, remain to be fully quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA coatings using identical processing methods: a control set with a near-stoichiometric composition that forms APDs and an experimental set with a slight compositional deviation designed to induce nanoscale precipitate formation. Subject both sets to standardized wear tests (e.g., pin-on-disk) under identical loads and temperature conditions. Conduct microstructural analysis (via TEM/SEM and XRD) to confirm the distribution and nature of the phases.
measurements: Wear rate (via mass or volume loss)
Microstructural characterization (TEM/SEM imaging and phase analysis)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experimental coatings with induced nanoscale precipitates do not statistically exhibit a significantly higher hardness and lower wear rate compared to the control APD coatings under identical testing conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Question: How can high-throughput computational screening be used to discover lightweight, precipitation-strengthened high-entropy alloys with high-temperature strength superior to traditional ferritic superalloys?. System: Al–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ti quinary system (specifically Al20Cr5Fe50Mn20Ti5 and Al15Cr5Fe50Mn25Ti5 as successful cases). Processing: Arc-melting of 99.9 wt% purity constituent elements, melted at least six times for homogeneity, followed by drop-casting; subsequent homogenization at 1200 °C and annealing at 700 °C for 2 hours for specific characterizations. Test conditions: Compression tests at room temperature and elevated temperatures (up to 700 °C) at a strain rate of 2 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹; in situ neutron scattering from room temperature to 1050 °C; synchrotron XRD and TEM characterization.
